old: I am absolutely in love with her beautiful little design
new: I am quite in raptures over her beautiful little design
source: I am quite in raptures with her beautiful little design for a table
reason: Darcy's reply in 10.15 ('save your raptures') picks up her word; with 'absolutely in love' the set-up for his dry retort is lost.

old: object of admiration to such a man
new: object of admiration to so great a man
source: she could be an object of admiration to so great a man
reason: 'great' (his rank and consequence) is the point of her disbelief; 'such a man' drops it and reads as distaste.

old: was considerably helped along by her desire
new: received some assistance from her desire
source: her great anxiety for the recovery of her dear friend Jane received some assistance from her desire of getting rid of Elizabeth
reason: Austen's ironic understatement ('some assistance') is inflated to 'considerably helped along', blunting the joke.

old: as soon as the cook has made enough white soup
new: as soon as Nicholls has made enough white soup
source: as soon as Nicholls has made white soup enough
reason: Named servant (Nicholls, the Netherfield housekeeper) replaced with an invented generic 'the cook'.

old: It is, I believe, too unforgiving—certainly too much so for the world's liking.
new: It is, I believe, too unyielding—certainly too much so for the world's convenience.
source: It is, I believe, too little yielding; certainly too little for the convenience of the world.
reason: 'too little yielding' means inflexible, not 'unforgiving'; the candidate pre-empts the resentment he confesses a few sentences later, and 'liking' changes 'convenience'.

old: every attempt to manipulate them
new: every attempt to move them
source: My feelings are not puffed about with every attempt to move them.
reason: 'move' means emotionally sway; 'manipulate' adds a sinister motive Darcy does not attribute to others.

old: Her reply, therefore, was not what Elizabeth had hoped for, though Elizabeth was eager to get home.
new: Her reply, therefore, was not favorable—at least not to Elizabeth's wishes, for she was eager to get home.
source: Her answer, therefore, was not propitious, at least not to Elizabeth's wishes, for she was impatient to get home.
reason: 'though' reverses the causal 'for'; Elizabeth's eagerness to go home is why the answer disappointed her.

old: when she knew she was right
new: when she felt she was right
source: Jane was firm where she felt herself to be right
reason: Certainty upgraded: source says she felt herself right, not that she knew it.

old: was sure Jane would catch cold again
new: was sure Jane would have caught cold again
source: was sure Jane would have caught cold again
reason: Mrs. Bennet is sure Jane already has caught cold again (her typical alarm), not predicting a future cold.

old: I think it is the most unjust thing in the world that your estate should be taken away from your own children.
new: I do think it is the hardest thing in the world that your estate should be entailed away from your own children.
source: I do think it is the hardest thing in the world, that your estate should be entailed away from your own children
reason: 'taken away' misstates the legal mechanism (the entail, explained in the next paragraph); 'hardest' is Mrs. Bennet's word, which Mr. Bennet's ironic 'most iniquitous' then escalates.

old: some family scruples on that point
new: some scruples as a dutiful son on that point
source: he does seem to have had some filial scruples on that head
reason: 'filial' means as a son toward his father (Collins's worry about disrespect to his father's memory); 'family' loses that.

old: otherwise they will be left with very little
new: otherwise they will be destitute enough
source: for else they will be destitute enough
reason: Mrs. Bennet's characteristic exaggeration ('destitute') is softened into a measured statement.

old: Lydia's mouth fell open as he opened the volume
new: Lydia yawned as he opened the volume
source: Lydia gaped as he opened the volume
reason: In Austen's usage 'gaped' here means yawned (boredom at Fordyce), not astonishment; the candidate reads it as surprise.

old: Mr. Collins was not a clever man
new: Mr. Collins was not a sensible man
source: Mr. Collins was not a sensible man
reason: 'sensible' (good sense/judgment) is not 'clever'; it answers Elizabeth's 'Can he be a sensible man, sir?' in 13.20 and Mr. Bennet's reply.

old: A fortunate recommendation had brought him
new: A fortunate chance had brought him
source: A fortunate chance had recommended him to Lady Catherine de Bourgh
reason: Source attributes his preferment to luck ('chance'); the candidate invents a recommendation, removing the jab.

old: a comparison that did not at first mean much to anyone
new: a comparison that did not at first seem much of a compliment
source: a comparison that did not at first convey much gratification
reason: The source point is that Mrs. Philips was not at first pleased (her drawing room likened to a small breakfast parlour), not that it meant nothing; this sets up 'she felt all the force of the compliment'.

old: rather than his betrayal of his father's wishes and disgrace to his father's memory
new: rather than his disappointing his father's hopes and disgracing his memory
source: rather than his disappointing the hopes and disgracing the memory of his father
reason: 'betrayal of his father's wishes' intensifies 'disappointing the hopes'.

old: a dislike that I can only attribute in part to jealousy
new: a dislike that I cannot help attributing in part to jealousy
source: a dislike which I cannot but attribute in some measure to jealousy
reason: 'can only attribute in part' reads as limiting (only partly jealousy); the source means he cannot help ascribing it partly to jealousy.

old: whose very face is proof of being good
new: whose very face might vouch for your good nature
source: whose very countenance may vouch for your being amiable
reason: Hedge 'may vouch' turned into flat 'is proof'; the modal is part of the irony of Elizabeth judging by looks.

old: pride has often been his best quality
new: pride has often been his best friend
source: pride has often been his best friend
reason: 'best friend' is Wickham's barbed idiom (pride has served him); 'best quality' turns it into a sincere compliment.

old: it is widely believed
new: it is believed
source: it is believed that she and her cousin will unite the two estates
reason: 'widely' adds a degree of public certainty to Wickham's report that the source does not claim.

old: if he was already destined for another
new: if he had already destined himself for another
source: if he were already self-destined to another
reason: 'self-destined' = Darcy's own choice; 'destined for' makes it an external arrangement.

old: should be considered first-rate
new: should have a first-rate mind
source: who chooses that everyone connected with him should have an understanding of the first class
reason: 'understanding' (intellect) is the point: Lady Catherine's reputation for cleverness; 'considered first-rate' is too general.

old: about the money she had lost and won
new: about the counters she had lost and won
source: of the fish she had lost and the fish she had won
reason: The 'fish' were game counters, not money; 'money' is a factual change.

old: he had really suffered such cruelty
new: he had really endured such unkindness
source: The possibility of his having really endured such unkindness
reason: 'cruelty' inflates Jane's gentle 'unkindness', out of keeping with her character.
